doc.title: Butch Miles interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Scottsdale, Arizona, March 4, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Al Grey calling out the charts
summary: Al Grey called out arrangement numbers each night, saving him while he learned the book; he still mixed up drum breaks on a couple of tunes.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: John Heard was telling us that his first night on the thing and he said “what tunes are we playing” and everybody in the band told him a different number, and he had to just like listen and see if he could do it, and apparently he did it.
Well I had an enormous amount of help. Because sitting immediately on my left was the fabulous Al Grey. Have you talked to Al yet?

Well he saved me. I’ll tell you right out front, Al Grey saved me, because no matter what intro Basie played, Al knew the number of the arrangement and would call out the arrangement. And while Basie is doodling around on the piano, everybody’s getting the chart up. And he saved me because of course I didn’t know any of the numbers. And there were about six or seven or eight pieces that I had no arrangement on at all, but fortunately I knew things like “Jumpin’ at the Woodside,” or “April in Paris,” “One O’clock Jump,” “Whirly Bird,” you know, a few of those, “Moten,” I never saw arrangements in the book. I don’t even know if there’d ever been a drum part written for those. But Al Grey absolutely saved my life every night, for so long, until I learned a lot of the book and I didn’t need the music in front of me anymore, when Al would call those numbers out. I don’t think he ever got one wrong, either. The memory was just amazing. It was incredible.
Well I can imagine that would be like an un-fun position to be in, like he’s playing this intro and you’re going, [gasp] now?

Well later it became a very fun position to be in, because I knew all the intros, and I knew most all the tunes except maybe some of the new ones that we’d just recorded the day before, the week before, we were all still scuffling and learning ourselves. But it was great. I could tell within one or two bars what the tune was going to be. But I’d still get them mixed up every once in a while, for some reason, I’d get the drum breaks on “Shiny Stockings” mixed up in my mind with the drum breaks on “Corner Pocket,” and I’d play the wrong break. I don’t know why, it would happen, I’d have a total lapse, complete lapse of memory, you know and just zoom right in there in the wrong place. But Basie © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-
never gave me a hard time about it. He’d just look at me or give me a face. “I’m sorry, Chief, I get it, I get it.”
